title: A Major Linux Project Voted Not to Ban AI Code
hook: Debian's answer to AI contributions: no special rules, no exemptions. If you submit it, you're accountable for it — same as always.
key_points: Debian voted to allow AI tools in development, maintenance, and documentation of the Linux distribution, per The Verge.
The policy says generative AI is 'neither exempt from nor subject to special rules beyond the standards already' in place.
The framing shifts the question from 'was AI used?' to 'does the contribution meet our bar?'
It acknowledges that 'responsible' AI use can improve developer productivity.
Practical upside: an AI-origin rule would be near-impossible to enforce, since detectors are unreliable.
content_html: Debian — one of the oldest and most influential Linux distributions, and the base for Ubuntu and many others — voted on whether to ban AI-generated contributions. It decided not to. The new policy lets developers use AI tools in the project's "development, maintenance, [and] documentation," acknowledging that responsible use can genuinely improve productivity.
extra_html:
The wording is the interesting part. Generative AI, the policy says, is "neither exempt from nor subject to special rules beyond the standards already" in place. That's a deliberate refusal to make AI a special category in either direction: no free pass for AI-assisted work, and no extra hurdle for it either. A contribution is judged by whether it's correct, maintainable, and properly licensed — the same bar it always faced.

There's a pragmatic reason this framing wins arguments. Origin-based bans require detecting origin, and AI detectors are notoriously unreliable — good enough to accuse people, not good enough to be right. Debian's version puts the weight on accountability instead: you submitted it, so you vouch for it. That's a template other volunteer projects, workplaces, and classrooms are likely to copy.

related.title: Using AI Responsibly
related.hook: The point of AI literacy isn't to use AI for everything — it's to use it well: check its work, be honest that you used it, and know the moments to put it down.

related.title: AI Detectors Are Making Everyone Suspicious of Everyone
related.hook: Tools that claim to spot AI writing are unreliable enough to flag honest work — and the damage isn't just false accusations. It's that nobody trusts anything anymore.

flashcards.prompt: What rule did Debian settle on for AI-assisted contributions?

choices.text: AI use is allowed and judged by the existing quality standards — no special rules either way
AI-generated code is allowed but exempt from normal review

flashcards.explanation_html: The policy states generative AI is "neither exempt from nor subject to special rules beyond the standards already" in place — contributions are judged on their merits.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'did you use AI?' a hard rule to enforce in practice?
flashcards.back_html: There's no reliable way to tell. AI-detection tools are inaccurate, so an origin-based ban would mostly generate false accusations, not compliance.

flashcards.prompt: What principle does Debian's approach put in place of a ban?
flashcards.back_html: Accountability. Whoever submits the work owns it and answers for its quality, regardless of what tools helped produce it.
